title: Sorghum, whole grain, white, dry, raw

content.title: About
content.content: Sorghum (Sorghum bicolor) is an annual cereal plant cultivated in warm regions worldwide. White whole grain, dry and raw, has a mild nutty flavor with a faint sweetness. Sorghum is used in cooking, food processing, and as animal feed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sorghum ranks as the fifth most produced cereal crop after wheat, rice, corn, and barley.
The grain is naturally gluten‑free, making it suitable for gluten‑free diets.
Ancient African and Asian civilizations relied on sorghum as a staple food and for ceremonial purposes.
Sorghum tolerates drought and can be grown with minimal irrigation.
Whole grain sorghum is processed into flour, grits, flakes, as well as spirits and bio‑fuel.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds such as quercetin help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The grain raises blood sugar slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for hemoglobin formation and muscle‑nerve function.

items.title: Good plant‑based protein
items.content: Sorghum provides about 10‑12 % protein, making it a valuable addition to vegetarian diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to sorghum.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting the grain is recommended.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Like other grains, sorghum may contain pesticide residues; choose certified organic products when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sorghum can be boiled as a grain, made into porridge, added to soups, baked, or ground into flour for breads and pastries. Before cooking, rinse and soak the grains for 4‑6 hours to improve flavor and digestibility.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry whole‑grain sorghum in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent mold growth and fat rancidity.
